tagline: Fisker Owners Association — check if your Ocean is ready for the Marlin update
intro_heading: Fisker Ocean software version completeness and Marlin Readiness test
intro_text: This analyzer will check if your car is completely updated to 2.1, 2.2 (including 2.2.2 + 2.2.3 = full 2.2) and if the car is ready for the Marlin software update.

privacy_text: This portal is run by volunteers for members of the Fisker Owners Association. When you upload a report it is analyzed on our server and the result is shown to you. To use the service you must accept that the report file, your VIN, the software versions of every control module, the country you uploaded from (from Cloudflare) and the upload time are stored in the association's vehicle register. The register is used to build aggregated statistics (number of cars per software status, version distribution per module) and to help the association plan updates; the public statistics page never shows individual VINs. The full register, including VINs, is available only to the association's administrators. No data is shared with third parties and no tracking cookies are used (only a cookie remembering your language choice). To have your data removed, contact the association; administrators can delete every record for a VIN. Separately from the register, each upload is also counted in an anonymous usage statistic for the administrators: country, language, outcome and a daily-changing hash for counting unique users. That count is not linked to the register entry and contains no VIN, no report and no IP address.
footer_disclaimer: Community tool — not affiliated with Fisker Inc. Updates are carried out by a service partner; confirm the result with them before an update is performed.
alpha_text: The check has been verified against real cars on 2.1, 2.2 and Marlin, but a few requirement values are still being confirmed by the association. Always confirm with a service partner before an update is performed.

how_intro: This page describes how the portal interprets your report and arrives at its verdict, which choices were made along the way, and what it does not tell you.

how_sections.title: What we read from the report
paragraphs: The report you upload is an “ECU Software Version Report” exported from the OceanLink Pro app. It lists the car’s control units, grouped by area (body, infotainment, powertrain, chassis and driver assistance), and gives four version fields for each unit. A typical report contains about 37 units.

The check uses one of those fields: Supplier SW Version. It is the field that states which software level the supplier delivered to each unit, and it is the level the association’s minimum requirements for Marlin are expressed in. The other fields are shown but do not count. The VIN is also read, for one reason only: its fifth character tells which trim the car is, and that decides which units are expected to be present.

A report is accepted only if it is a genuine OLP export with the heading, a VIN and at least one control unit. If anything is missing, the file is rejected with an explanation instead of the car getting a verdict on shaky ground.

how_sections.title: From text to numbers
paragraphs: Supplier SW Version is a text that looks different from supplier to supplier, for example “BCM395030”, “VCU039021”, “ECC395 24” or a long string for the stability system. The requirements, however, are numbers. The check therefore has a pattern per unit that says which part of the text is the product code and which part is the actual level. For BCM the level is the last digits, for ESP it is three digits after the letter V, and so on.

The patterns were built from real reports from cars on 2.1, 2.2 and Marlin, and every value we have seen is interpreted correctly. If a text turns up that the pattern does not recognise, the unit gets the status “version not recognised”, which counts as not approved. That is a deliberate choice: the check must never say “ready” on the basis of something it does not understand. If the field is empty in the report, the unit gets its own status saying exactly that, so you can see the problem is in the report, not in the car.

how_sections.title: The requirements and the verdict
paragraphs: The requirements are organised by software release: 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2. For each of the seven units that matter for Marlin, body control (BCM), stability system (ESP), climate control (ECC), battery management (BMS), front and rear motor control (MCU) and vehicle control (VCU), the table states the minimum level a unit must have to belong to each release. The result page shows this table with one column per release and a tick or cross per unit.

The check first works out how far the car has come. A release is “complete” when all seven units are at its level or higher. It also looks at whether any unit already carries a level that only a higher release installs; where two releases share the same minimum for a unit (climate control is 24 on both 2.1 and 2.2, for instance) that unit is never taken as proof of the higher release.

From that, the car gets one of five results. “2.2 fully updated”: every unit at the 2.2 level, Marlin ready. “2.1 fully updated”: every unit at 2.1 and none at 2.2 — Marlin is possible, but the units the 2.2 update lifts would stay behind, so 2.2 first is recommended. “2.2 zebra”: everything at least 2.1, some units already at 2.2 and others not — a started but incomplete 2.2; finish it, then Marlin. “2.1 zebra”: at least one unit below 2.1 — not Marlin ready; lift those units to 2.1, then 2.2, then Marlin. And “already on Marlin” for cars whose vehicle controller shows the Marlin level. In every case the page lists the units that are holding the car back, with the number read and the number required.

how_sections.title: One unit, two software lines
paragraphs: Battery management comes in two independent variants, because the cars have two different battery types: one line for the NMC pack in One, Extreme and Ultra, and one for the LFP pack in Sport. The numbers in the two lines cannot be compared with each other, so each line has its own minimum. The check picks the line from what the report actually shows, not from what kind of car it assumes. If the text starts with anything other than the two known lines, the unit is “not recognised”.

how_sections.title: The trim from the VIN
paragraphs: The fifth character of the VIN tells which trim the car is: Z for One, E for Extreme, U for Ultra and S for Sport. The check uses it for one thing. The Sport has a single motor and therefore no rear motor controller, so for a Sport it is not an error that this unit is missing. For every other trim, a missing rear motor controller is an error.

If the fifth character is a letter the check does not know, every unit is required. It never guesses in the direction that something is fine to be missing. The trim is shown on the result page so you can react if it is wrong.

how_sections.title: Cars that already run Marlin
paragraphs: Marlin gives the vehicle controller (VCU) level 24, “VCU 2.4”, which no earlier release has. If the report shows VCU 24 or higher, the car gets the verdict “already on Marlin” instead of ready or zebra, since the question of updating no longer applies. The table is shown for information, together with a list of units that are still below the 2.2 level. Marlin does not update every unit, and it can be useful to know which ones are left behind.

how_sections.title: Units without requirements
paragraphs: The roughly thirty units that are not among the seven are shown under “other units” with their values, but do not affect the verdict. That includes the radars, the front camera and the driver-assistance unit, which are not a prerequisite for Marlin and which we have seen at older levels on cars where Marlin and driver assistance work fine. Right-hand-drive cars have their own software lines on some units, but none of them are among the seven, so they are treated the same.

bullets.text: Everything the check does not understand, an unknown format, an empty field, a missing unit or an unknown trim, counts against the car. Better one zebra too many than one false “ready”.

bullets.lead: The requirements come from the association.
bullets.text: The minimum levels are the association’s Marlin table, checked against real reports from cars sitting exactly at the 2.1 minimums, on full 2.2 and on Marlin. Some values, among them the Sport battery, rest on fewer cars and are being confirmed as more reports come in. The requirements can be updated without rebuilding the check, and the requirements version used is printed on every result.

The whole interpretation is fixed rules and patterns. The same report always gives the same answer, and every number on the result page can be traced to one line in the report and one number in the requirements.

The result is available for 30 minutes behind a link nobody can guess. The report, the VIN and every module version go into the association's vehicle register, which its administrators use for statistics and update planning; the public statistics never show individual cars. See the privacy page for what is stored and how to have it removed.

how_sections.title: What the check does not tell you
paragraphs: It does not assess hardware versions, bootloaders or whether units are faulty, and it does not say whether an update will succeed, only whether the prerequisites in the association’s table are met. Updates are carried out by a service partner. Bring the result along when you contact them, so they can see which units need attention first.

steps_heading: This is what you do to have your car analyzed
intro_steps: Connect to OLP (OceanLink Pro) with the green OBD-II dongle (Bluetooth 4.0, plugged into the car's diagnostic port), run OLP diagnostics mode (lower left icon), click the software version icon and run the software version report (all ECUs). Save the PDF report to a folder on your phone (for example Files or Downloads), or email it to yourself, open the email on a computer and save the attachment to a folder there — whichever is easiest. In step 2 you pick the file from that folder.

Click “Choose file” below and pick the OLP report, either from that folder on your phone or from the computer you emailed it to. The PDF file is called “ecu_software_report_…”. Tick the box to allow your VIN and ECU versions to be stored in the association's vehicle register, and press Analyze.
